area: V2X communication network/channel realism (SOTA 2024-2026) for a pure-Python SCMS simulator on Windows
findings:
CONTEXT (repo): current model = hard disc default + opt-in radio_model="logdistance" (mean RX power = 10*n*log10(range/d) dB rel. sensitivity + i.i.d. per-link log-normal shadowing), with packet_loss_base/nlos_loss/congestion/weather composed as per-packet drops (tests/test_radio_propagation.py; OSM buildings already imported in src/scms_sim_ref/mock_pipeline/osm.py). The research below maps directly onto upgrading this.

== 1. FULL NETWORK SIMULATORS (the fidelity ceiling) ==
- Veins 5.3 (veins.car2x.org; github.com/sommer/veins/releases): OMNeT++ 802.11p PHY/MAC + IEEE 1609.4, SUMO/TraCI coupling. Compatible with OMNeT++ 6.1.0/6.0.3/5.7.1. Ships the standard "Simple Obstacle Shadowing" empirical building model (Sommer et al., WONS 2011, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5720204/): attenuation = beta*(number of exterior walls crossed) + gamma*(meters traversed inside buildings), calibrated from real 802.11p measurements (typical config: ~9 dB per wall + 0.4 dB/m), validated "very high accuracy ... marginal overhead". Windows: Veins core builds natively with OMNeT++'s bundled toolchain, but veins_inet (INET coupling) is "only supported when built using the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)" (https://veins.car2x.org/download/).
- Artery (github.com/riebl/artery; http://artery.v2x-research.eu/): ETSI ITS-G5 full stack via Vanetza (GeoNetworking, BTP, CAM/DENM/CPM facilities, access-layer DCC), middleware/services architecture, Veins or INET radios. Contains a from-scratch C++ GEMV^2 implementation (http://artery.v2x-research.eu/features/gemv2/): NLOSb corner diffractions + one-fold wall reflections, NLOSf foliage attenuation, building polygons from OSM, R-trees — but only usable with the INET radio model. Linux-oriented (Docker on Windows).
- ns-3 ecosystem: the old src/wave (WAVE/1609) module is gone from current ns-3 (deprecated 802.11p code removed from wifi via Bug 945; 802.11p OFDM 10 MHz remains in the wifi module). V2V channel: ThreeGppV2vUrban/HighwayPropagationLossModel implement 3GPP TR 37.885 Table 6.2.1-1 (see §2), plus NakagamiPropagationLossModel (three distance bands m0/m1/m2 at Distance1=80 m, Distance2=200 m; classic defaults m=1.5/0.75/0.75) (https://www.nsnam.org/docs/models/html/propagation.html). Windows: ns-3 officially targets Linux/macOS; WSL2 is the practical Windows path.
- ms-van3t (Politecnico di Torino; paper: "ms-van3t: An integrated multi-stack framework for virtual validation of V2X communication and services", Computer Communications 217 (2024), https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140366424000227): multi-stack ns-3 framework with IEEE 802.11p, LTE, LTE-V2X (C-V2X mode 4) and NR-V2X mode 2 under one ETSI-compliant facilities layer (ASN.1 CAM/DENM/CPM/VAM), SUMO TraCI + CARLA co-simulation (ms-van3t-CARLA, WONS 2024, https://www.eurecom.fr/publication/7556/download/comsys-publi-7556.pdf). 802.11bd planned. Linux only.
- VaN3Twin (github.com/DriveX-devs/VaN3Twin, 2025): the renamed successor that "integrates the whole ms-van3t framework, and much more" — adds NVIDIA Sionna RT ray-tracing channel integration (Blender/Mitsuba scenes, Doppler-aware), a TxTracker co-channel coexistence/interference module simulating 802.11p and NR-V2X simultaneously in one band, adaptive ETSI DCC, CARLA integration. Platform: Ubuntu 20.04/22.04/24.04 only — Windows unsupported.
- 5G-LENA NR-V2X (CTTC, https://5g-lena.cttc.es/features/; apps.nsnam.org/app/nr/): NR sidelink/V2X in a separate branch; latest V2X release compatible with 5G-LENA v3.1 + ns-3.42 (July 2024). Implements NR frame structure, PSCCH/PSSCH, mode 2 autonomous (sensing-based SPS) resource selection, FR1 numerologies 0-2, out-of-coverage. System-level evaluation papers: "3GPP NR V2X Mode 2: Overview, Models and System-Level Evaluation" (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10350958/), MAC PRR model validated vs ns-3 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.16680).
- Eclipse MOSAIC (https://eclipse.dev/mosaic/, github.com/eclipse-mosaic/mosaic): Java core runs on Windows natively. Built-in SNS (Simple Network Simulator, https://eclipse.dev/mosaic/docs/simulators/network_simulator_sns/): singlehop broadcast/unicast + geo-casts, SimpleAdhocTransmissionModel (configured delay + lossProbability, hop count always 1) or SophisticatedAdhocTransmissionModel (greedy forwarding + flooding chains), delay models (ConstantDelay default 0 ms, SimpleRandomDelay, GammaRandomDelay), singlehopRadius default 509.4 m, maximumTtl 10, maxRetries. SNS explicitly does NOT model MAC contention, fading, or antennas — i.e., MOSAIC's built-in network realism is BELOW what this repo already has with logdistance+shadowing. High-fidelity federates: ns-3 federate supports only ns-3.36.1 and is Linux-only ("with WSL ... possible to use the ns-3 federate ... in a Windows environment", https://eclipse.dev/mosaic/docs/simulators/network_simulator_ns3/); OMNeT++ federate supports only OMNeT++ 5.5 + INET 4.1 and runs on Windows only via Docker (https://eclipse.dev/mosaic/docs/simulators/network_simulator_omnetpp/). Both federate versions are dated (current ns-3 is 3.42+).
- Others: OpenCV2X (OMNeT++/SimuLTE C-V2X mode 4 reference), Artery-C for cellular V2X (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.05724); WiLabV2Xsim (github.com/V2Xgithub/WiLabV2Xsim; MATLAB, evolved from LTEV2Vsim): open-source system-level simulator of LTE-V2X mode 4 SPS, NR-V2X mode 2 and 802.11p CSMA/CA with 37.885-style channels — MATLAB code is directly portable to Python and is a common PRR-vs-distance benchmark generator.

== 2. CHANNEL MODELS — exact equations/parameters ==
(a) 3GPP TR 37.885 (V2X evaluation methodology; exact constants verified from the ns-3 implementation, https://www.qkdnetsim.info/html/d8/de1/three-gpp-v2v-propagation-loss-model_8cc_source.html and https://atisorg.s3.amazonaws.com/archive/3gpp-documents/Rel15/ATIS.3GPP.37.885.V1530.pdf):
  Urban LOS: PL = 38.77 + 16.7*log10(d3D) + 18.2*log10(f_GHz).
  Urban NLOS: PL = 36.85 + 30*log10(d3D) + 18.9*log10(f_GHz).
  Highway LOS: PL = 32.4 + 20*log10(d3D) + 20*log10(f_GHz) (NLOS/NLOSv reuse urban formulas).
  NLOSv (LOS path blocked by a vehicle, same street): PL = PL_LOS + additional loss = max{0, N(mu,sigma)} where: both antennas below blocker height -> mu = 9.0 + max(0, 15*log10(d3D) - 41), sigma = 4.5 dB; one antenna below -> mu = 5.0 + max(0, 15*log10(d3D) - 41), sigma = 4.0 dB; both above blocker -> 0. Blocker heights: cars 1.6 m, trucks 3.0 m (drawn per truck proportion).
  Shadow fading sigma: 3.0 dB (LOS and NLOSv), 4.0 dB (NLOS); spatial autocorrelation distance 10 m (LOS) / 13 m (NLOSv, NLOS). Link state re-evaluated at each 100 ms location update.
(b) 3GPP TR 36.885 (LTE-V2X eval): urban V2V LOS uses WINNER+ B1 Manhattan-grid microcell (fit A=22.7, B=41.0, C=20 at 5.9 GHz), i.i.d.-per-link log-normal shadowing with exponential (Gudmundson) autocorrelation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10145061/).
(c) ETSI TR 103 257-1 V1.1.1 (2019, "Analysis of V2X radio channel models", https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_tr/103200_103299/10325701/01.01.01_60/tr_10325701v010101p.pdf): recommends ITU-R multiple-knife-edge diffraction for multi-vehicle blockage; urban model with log-normal correlated shadowing sigma = 3 dB and 10 m decorrelation distance — adopted by ITS-G5 simulation studies (e.g., https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.09510).
(d) GEMV^2 (Boban et al., IEEE TVT 2014, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1305.0124; code: https://vehicle2x.net/ MATLAB, free; manual https://vehicle2x.net/wp-content/UserManual1.2/UserManual1.2.html; ns-3 port github.com/rocktale/gemv2-ns3; C++ port in Artery): per-link geometric classification into LOS / NLOSv (vehicles) / NLOSb (buildings) / NLOSf (foliage) using R-trees over OSM building+foliage outlines and vehicle rectangles; large-scale: LOS = two-ray ground reflection; NLOSv = multiple knife-edge diffraction over obstructing vehicles (ITU-R method); NLOSb = log-distance + single reflections off building walls + corner diffractions; small-scale: zero-mean normal whose sigma is scaled between min/max by the number/size of surrounding objects. Validated against measurement campaigns in highway/urban/suburban/open environments; scales to "tens of thousands of objects ... hundreds of thousands of communicating pairs" in MATLAB. This is the acknowledged SOTA "realism per CPU cycle" model and its inputs (SUMO positions + OSM polygons) match this repo exactly.
(e) Measured log-distance parameters, 5.9 GHz: Cheng/Henty/Stancil (suburban Pittsburgh DSRC, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/3236681): dual-slope log-distance with breakpoint (~100 m); Nakagami m fitted per distance bin, m high (~3) near, decaying toward 1 (occasionally sub-Rayleigh m<1 at long range). Karedal et al. "Pathloss modeling for V2V communications" report LOS exponents ~1.7-1.9 (waveguiding in streets can push n below 2). Abbas et al. shadow-fading model (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1203.3370) introduces the LOS/OLOS (obstructed-LOS) two-state approach for highways. Urban intersections: Mangel et al. VirtualSource11p (EURASIP JWCN 2011, open access https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1687-1499-2011-182, validated at 8 Munich intersections, best paper ITST 2011): closed-form NLOS path loss from ds, dr (distances to intersection center) and street geometry, "computationally light", the de-facto intersection model in packet-level simulators (used by Veins as well); multilink intersection measurements (Sensors 18(12):4433, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6308981/) report NLOS shadow sigma 4.39 dB (car-car) to 5.57 dB (truck-obstructed), decorrelation distances 2.2-3.7 m.
(f) Vehicle blockage measurements: a single blocking vehicle costs 5.5-17 dB depending on blocker size (multi-band V2V blockage characterization, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/330330604) — the empirical basis for 37.885's NLOSv mu of 5-9 dB; Boban's earlier JSAC work found ~10 dB typical for one obstructing vehicle.
(g) Sionna RT (NVIDIA, github.com/NVlabs/sionna-rt): differentiable ray tracer on Mitsuba 3/Dr.Jit, pip-installable Python; CPU (LLVM) mode works on native Windows, CUDA ray tracing NOT supported on native Windows and OptiX not in WSL2 (github.com/NVlabs/sionna/issues/593). ns3-rt integrates it into ns-3 (github.com/robpegurri/ns3-rt); VaN3Twin uses it. SOTA for site-specific deterministic channels, but scene prep (Blender/Mitsuba) and per-pair tracing cost make it a validation tool, not a per-tick engine for large fleets.

== 3. MAC / SYSTEM LEVEL: 802.11p vs C-V2X mode 4, congestion, hidden terminals ==
- 802.11p broadcast MAC = DCF CSMA/CA without ACK/RTS-CTS/retransmission — one shot per CAM/BSM; losses come from: signal below carrier-sense, SNR too low (propagation), and collisions (simultaneous backoff expiry + hidden terminals). Hidden-terminal + congestion behavior analyzed in "IEEE 802.11p-based Packet Broadcast in Radio Channels with Hidden Stations and Congestion Control" (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.03449). SOTA closed-form treatment: Sepulcre et al., "Analytical Models of the Performance of IEEE 802.11p Vehicle to Vehicle Communications" (IEEE TVT 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07923): models PDR(d) via the four packet-error types AND is "the first analytical model capable to accurately estimate the Channel Busy Ratio (CBR) ... even under high channel load"; inputs: vehicle density, beacon rate, power, data rate, packet size, pathloss model; validated against simulation over wide parameter ranges; open implementation published.
- C-V2X mode 4 (LTE-V2X) sensing-based SPS: reselection counter drawn 5-15 (at 100 ms RRI; scaled for other RRIs), probability of keeping resources p_keep in [0, 0.8], 1000 ms sensing window, RSRP exclusion threshold raised in 3 dB steps until >=20% of resources remain candidates, selection from the best 20%. Canonical analytical model: Gonzalez-Martin, Sepulcre, Molina-Masegosa, Gozalvez, "Analytical Models of the Performance of C-V2X Mode 4 Vehicular Communications" (IEEE TVT 68(2) 2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06508): PDR(d) decomposed into four error types — half-duplex (HD), below-sensing-power (SEN), propagation (PRO), collision (COL) — validated against a full network simulator; open MATLAB: https://github.com/msepulcre/C-V2X (straightforward Python port). Key modeling differences vs 802.11p: half-duplex misses (a node cannot receive while transmitting in its subframe), deterministic periodic collisions between nodes that picked the same resource (persist until counter expiry — error floor), no carrier-sense collisions, 10/20 MHz subchannelization, HARQ blind retransmission option.
- First open C-V2X mode 4 simulator: Eckermann et al. (ns-3, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.09977). SPS-only lightweight simulators exist (github.com/xinuvic/Simulators-for-SPS, ms-level, periodic+aperiodic traffic).
- ETSI DCC (access layer, ITS-G5): TS 102 687 V1.2.1 (2018, https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/102600_102699/102687/01.02.01_60/ts_102687v010201p.pdf). CBR = fraction of 100-ms-window probes with power above threshold (-85 dBm). Reactive state machine (as commonly implemented, e.g. in VaN3Twin/ms-van3t): Relaxed CBR<0.30 -> 10 Hz (Toff 100 ms); Active1 0.30-0.40 -> 5 Hz (200 ms); Active2 0.40-0.50 -> 2.5 Hz (400 ms); Active3 0.50-0.60 -> 2 Hz (500 ms); Restrictive CBR>0.60 -> 1 Hz (1000 ms). Adaptive approach (LIMERIC-derived): delta(n) = (1-alpha)*delta(n-1) + beta*(CBR_target - CBR(n)) with alpha=0.016, beta=0.0012, CBR_target=0.68, delta capped at delta_max=0.03 of channel time, updated every 200 ms (sources: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.01297, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.12089). Known dynamics: good utilization but slow convergence/transient unfairness (Bansal et al. critique). C-V2X congestion control: ETSI TS 103 574 CBR/CR (channel-occupancy-ratio) limits per 3GPP 36.213 (survey: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.04871).

== 4. MEASUREMENT CAMPAIGNS USABLE AS CALIBRATION REFERENCES ==
- Safety Pilot Model Deployment (Ann Arbor, world's largest CV test; "Empirical Study of DSRC Performance", IEEE T-ITS 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08365): quantifies effective range and PDR degradation from trees/foliage, weather, buildings, travel direction, road elevation; defines Effective Range = distance where PDR>=50%.
- FLOURISH Bristol ITS-G5 dataset (Data in Brief 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6727192/, arxiv 1903.10289): 4 RSUs on a 5 km central-Bristol track, 2 OBUs, 8 x ~2 h sessions, CAMs every 10 ms at 25 dBm (LP) and 29 dBm (HP); provides empirical MAC-layer PDR-as-function-of-RSSI curves "suitable for calibrating physical layers of vehicular simulators"; open data DOI 10.5523/bris.eupowp7h3jl525yxhm3521f57.
- Boban & d'Orey, "Exploring the Practical Limits of Cooperative Awareness" (https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.06590; measurements at 4 EU sites + GEMV2 large-scale simulation): 90% awareness achievable up to ~200 m urban and >500 m highway; delivery dominated by shadowing (power beats rate).
- Urban V2I 802.11p (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/254058759): max range with frame-success-ratio continuously >0.25 is ~700 m in urban V2I.
- GEMV^2 validation sets (Porto/Lund measurements) and the WiLabV2Xsim / msepulcre analytical-model outputs serve as reproducible PDR(d) reference curves for highway densities (802.11p vs C-V2X mode 4 cross-over behavior: mode 4 wins at long range/low load via HARQ+lower MCS, degrades under SPS collisions at high density).

== 5. KEY QUESTION — what is realistically implementable in PURE PYTHON ==
The literature consensus stack that is implementable in pure Python at O(n log n)/step cost:
(1) GEMV^2-style geometric link classification using the repo's existing OSM building polygons + vehicle rectangles (shapely STRtree; GEMV2 itself uses R-trees and handles tens of thousands of objects in MATLAB — numpy+shapely matches that);
(2) per-class large-scale loss: either GEMV2 sub-models (two-ray LOS, knife-edge NLOSv, log-distance+reflection/diffraction NLOSb) or, simpler and standards-anchored, the exact 3GPP TR 37.885 formulas above + VirtualSource11p at intersections;
(3) spatially correlated shadowing: per-link Gudmundson/AR(1) process, sigma 3/3/4 dB, decorrelation 10-13 m (25 m highway), instead of i.i.d. draws;
(4) small-scale fading: per-packet Nakagami-m draw with distance-dependent m (e.g., 3 / 1.5 / 1.0 over 0-50 / 50-150 / >150 m bands, ns-3-style), mapped through an SINR->PER curve for the 6 Mb/s QPSK-1/2 10 MHz 802.11p profile;
(5) MAC/congestion WITHOUT event-level simulation: port the validated closed-form models — Sepulcre 2022 for 802.11p (CBR, hidden-terminal/collision, sensing errors) and Gonzalez-Martin 2019 for C-V2X mode 4 (HD/SEN/PRO/COL, open MATLAB) — giving per-distance loss probabilities as a function of local density/rate/power;
(6) ETSI DCC feedback loop (reactive table and/or adaptive alpha=0.016/beta=0.0012/target 0.68) modulating CAM rate from modeled CBR.
What genuinely requires a real network simulator (ns-3/OMNeT++): symbol-accurate PHY (coded BER, capture effect timing, HARQ combining), exact EDCA queue/backoff microbehavior and per-packet SPS grant dynamics, GeoNetworking multi-hop/CBF forwarding, NR numerology detail, and cross-technology co-channel interference (VaN3Twin territory). For broadcast CAM/BSM safety beaconing — the SCMS use case — the analytical models reproduce full-simulator PDR(d) curves closely (both papers validate against comprehensive simulators over wide parameter ranges), so the marginal realism of a coupled network simulator is small relative to its cost, and on this Windows host every high-fidelity option (ns-3, ms-van3t, VaN3Twin, Artery, MOSAIC ns-3 federate) needs WSL2/Docker anyway; only Veins-core (native OMNeT++) and MOSAIC's Java core+SNS run natively, and SNS is less realistic than the repo's existing model.
benchmarks: 3GPP TR 37.885 pathloss reproduction: Urban LOS PL=38.77+16.7log10(d)+18.2log10(f_GHz); Urban NLOS PL=36.85+30log10(d)+18.9log10(f_GHz); Highway LOS PL=32.4+20log10(d)+20log10(f_GHz); shadowing sigma 3 dB (LOS/NLOSv) / 4 dB (NLOS); decorrelation 10 m LOS / 13 m NLOS; link state update every 100 ms

NLOSv vehicle-blockage extra loss: max{0,N(mu,sigma)} with mu=9+max(0,15log10(d)-41) dB, sigma=4.5 dB (both antennas below blocker) or mu=5+..., sigma=4.0 dB (one below); blocker heights 1.6 m car / 3.0 m truck; measured single-vehicle blockage 5.5-17 dB (~10 dB typical)

PDR/awareness vs distance: 90% cooperative awareness up to ~200 m urban and >500 m highway (Boban 2015, measurement+GEMV2); urban V2I max range ~700 m at frame-success-ratio 0.25; Safety Pilot 'effective range' = distance where PDR>=50%
Empirical PDR-vs-RSSI calibration curve from FLOURISH Bristol ITS-G5 dataset (4 RSUs, 5 km urban track, CAMs @100 Hz, 25/29 dBm; open dataset DOI 10.5523/bris.eupowp7h3jl525yxhm3521f57)

Nakagami-m fading vs distance: m~3 below ~50 m falling toward m=1 (Rayleigh) beyond ~150-200 m (Cheng/Henty/Stancil 5.9 GHz dual-slope with ~100 m breakpoint; ns-3 default bands m=1.5/0.75/0.75 at 80/200 m)
Building shadowing (Veins/Sommer WONS 2011, measurement-validated): attenuation = ~9 dB per exterior wall crossed + ~0.4 dB per meter of interior propagation
Urban intersection NLOS: VirtualSource11p closed-form model (validated at 8 Munich intersections); measured intersection shadow sigma 4.39-5.57 dB with 2.2-3.7 m decorrelation distance

ETSI reactive DCC state table: CBR<0.30 relaxed 10 Hz; 0.30-0.40 5 Hz; 0.40-0.50 2.5 Hz; 0.50-0.60 2 Hz; >0.60 restrictive 1 Hz (Toff 100/200/400/500/1000 ms); adaptive DCC converges CBR to 0.68 with alpha=0.016, beta=0.0012, delta_max=0.03, 200 ms updates; CBR = share of 100-ms probes above -85 dBm

PDR error decomposition targets: 802.11p PDR(d) = f(below-sensing, propagation, collision incl. hidden terminal) with CBR accurate at high load (Sepulcre TVT 2022); C-V2X mode 4 PDR(d) = f(half-duplex, sensing, propagation, SPS collision) (Gonzalez-Martin TVT 2019) — both validated against full network simulators
C-V2X mode 4 SPS parameters: reselection counter 5-15 (100 ms RRI), p_keep in [0,0.8], 1000 ms sensing window, RSRP threshold stepped +3 dB until >=20% candidate resources

GEMV^2 scalability yardstick: tens of thousands of objects / hundreds of thousands of link pairs per timestep in MATLAB using R-trees — a pure-Python shapely-STRtree port should meet or beat this with numpy vectorization

tools.name: VirtualSource11p (Mangel et al. 2011)
tools.what: Closed-form validated 5.9 GHz NLOS intersection pathloss from street geometry; designed for packet-level simulators
tools.maturity: Classic, validated (8 Munich intersections), used inside Veins
tools.integration_effort: Low: ~30 lines, pairs naturally with OSM intersection geometry

recommendations: 1. Build a GEMV^2-style geometric channel in pure Python as the new opt-in radio_model: classify each link LOS/NLOSv/NLOSb per tick using shapely STRtree over the repo's existing OSM building polygons + vehicle rectangles, then apply the exact 3GPP TR 37.885 pathloss constants (urban LOS 38.77+16.7log10 d+18.2log10 f; NLOS 36.85+30log10 d+18.9log10 f; highway LOS 32.4+20log10 d+20log10 f) with the NLOSv additional-loss distribution (mu=5..9+max(0,15log10 d-41), sigma 4.0-4.5 dB). This is the highest realism-per-effort step and is fully Windows-native.

2. Replace i.i.d. shadowing with spatially correlated shadowing: per-link AR(1)/Gudmundson process, sigma 3 dB (LOS/NLOSv) / 4 dB (NLOS), decorrelation 10-13 m urban (ETSI TR 103 257-1 uses 3 dB/10 m) — burst losses and re-hearing dynamics change materially vs i.i.d. draws.

3. Add per-packet Nakagami-m small-scale fading with distance-dependent m (~3 below 50 m, ~1.5 mid, 1.0 beyond ~150 m per Cheng et al./ns-3 practice) feeding an SINR->PER mapping for the 6 Mb/s QPSK-1/2 802.11p profile, replacing the flat packet_loss_base on closed links.

4. Port the validated closed-form MAC models instead of simulating the MAC: Sepulcre et al. 2022 for 802.11p (CBR + hidden-terminal/collision/sensing error probabilities vs local density and rate) and, if C-V2X matters, Gonzalez-Martin et al. 2019 mode 4 model (HD/SEN/PRO/COL; open MATLAB at github.com/msepulcre/C-V2X). This turns the 'congestion' knob into physics that responds to fleet density and beacon rate.

5. Implement ETSI DCC as a feedback loop on modeled CBR: reactive table (10/5/2.5/2/1 Hz at CBR 0.30/0.40/0.50/0.60 breakpoints) and adaptive LIMERIC (alpha=0.016, beta=0.0012, target CBR 0.68, 200 ms updates) — a security-relevant behavior for SCMS scenarios (DCC-induced rate drops alter misbehavior-detection evidence density).

6. Encode published curves as regression tests in the existing golden-digest style: 90% awareness at ~200 m urban / >500 m highway (Boban 2015), PDR>=50% effective-range behavior (Safety Pilot), monotone PDR(d) family per density, and calibrate the PER mapping against the open FLOURISH Bristol PDR-vs-RSSI dataset.

7. Do NOT federate with a network simulator in-loop on this Windows host: MOSAIC's native-Windows path (SNS) is less realistic than the current logdistance model, and its ns-3/OMNeT++ federates are dated (ns-3 3.36.1, OMNeT++ 5.5) and need WSL/Docker. Instead, stand up ms-van3t or VaN3Twin in WSL2 once, offline, to generate cross-validation PDR(d)/CBR traces for a handful of canonical scenarios.

8. Optional stretch: use Sionna RT (CPU mode works natively on Windows) to spot-check the geometric model's LOS/NLOS classification and pathloss on one or two real OSM scenes; add VirtualSource11p as the intersection-specific NLOS refinement (~30 lines).
